Precious Metals Quarterly 2012 Q1 

# Executive summary 

## Palladium:  large deficits become the new market reality 

Having moved into deficit in 2010 for the first time in seven years, the palladium market was brought back into large surplus in 2011, even though, at the fundamental level, fabrication demand was still higher than mine and scrap supply.  Unlike in 2010, the fundamental drivers were largely ignored by market players as both wild cards inherent to the palladium market – investment demand and Russian state sales – came back into play. 



- In the next five years, we do not foresee any technological developments which could jeopardise the dominant role of the internal combustion engine and therefore threaten demand for palladium in catalytic converters. 



- Automakers in China, Japan and North America will continue consuming palladium in ever increasing volumes, providing strong price support.  Although demand from Europe is expected to stumble this year, this too will resuming an upward trajectory in 2013. 



- Demand from the electronics industry is expected to continue growing until the end of our forecast horizon, supported by growth in production of multi-layer ceramic capacitors.  The chemicals industry will also contribute to the growth in demand, although we do not expect this to kick in before 2015. 



- Overall, total palladium demand is forecast to grow in each of the next five years, at a compound annual rate of 6%. 



- Palladium mine production is set to grow at a compound annual rate of only 1.3% between 2012 and 2016.  Within this period, output is expected to contract in 2012 and 2013 before growth resumes in 2014.  Rising mining costs, falling grades, mine safety issues, strikes and other industrial actions will be the major limiting factors. 



- Russian state stocks of palladium are expected to become less important in terms of the palladium supply-demand balance in the years ahead. 



- As witnessed last year, strong fundamentals do not always guarantee strong price performance.  Therefore, investment demand will be vital in determining the future direction of the price. 



- We expect that palladium’s bull run will continue over the next five years with the real price averaging $987/oz over the period.

## Other precious metal markets 

#### Gold 

Gold’s market surplus is likely to expand over the next two years, driven by weakening fabrication demand and growing mine supply.  However, after peaking in 2013, the surplus may then decline during the 2014-16 period, driven by slowing mine production, tighter scrap supplies and stronger demand for jewellery caused by lower prices and rising incomes. 



- Investor interest is stabilising while central bank buying continues to provide support, but greater market stresses are now needed to drive each fresh wave of buying interest. 



- Imposition of highe

r import duty on gold imports in India will reduce local and global demand for gold and may cost the country its title of the largest gold jewellery consumer. 

#### Silver 

After suffering more than gold in 2011 Q4, with the gold:silver price ratio rising from 53 to 59 in December, silver began to benefit from its industrial metal credentials early in 2012 as nervousness about the global economy has let up a little.  However, investor demand will still drive future prices. 



- Despite a slight improvement in sentiment towards the economy in recent months, we have cut our projections of economic activity in each of the next five years.  This has reduced our estimate of total offtake in 2016 by 275 tonnes so that demand now grows to 29,450 tonnes. 



- Although projects have been proceeding, finance is hard to come by on terms that are 

- acceptable to potential producers.  We believe that this, as well as lower prices, will help to hold Western output back behind its full potential in 2016 by about 2,000 tonnes. 



- With interest rates unlikely to begin rising notably in 2014, we do expect silver’s price to fall before then.  Even then, we believe that the market will be running a surplus of about 4,000 t/y. 

#### Platinum 

Unlike in our December forecast, we now foresee the platinum market shifting into fundamental deficit in 2014. 



- Taking into account the strong likelihood of a return to recession this year for many European countries, demand for platinum in this key region is likely to decline before it starts growing again. 



- The supply of platinum remains constrained.  The sharp decline in the platinum price from mid- to late 2011 prompted some South African platinum miners to cut production and reduce their capital expenditure. 



- Since last September platinum has been trading largely at a discount to gold due to the grim outlook for the global economy and industrial demand.

## Data sources and study team 

The historical data presented in this report are based on estimates published by a variety of sources, including Johnson Matthey (JM), World Gold Council (WGC), International Financial Statistics (IFS), JD Power, London Bullion Market Association (LBMA), World Bureau of Metal Statistics (WBMS), GTIS trade statistics, and company websites and written reports. 

However, CRU’s interpretation of these data may or may not coincide with those expressed in these various sources. 

The forecast is exclusively CRU’s.
